strengths: The Gaussian classification problem has an identifiable interested audience. Sparsity of whitened mean differences offers a useful perspective distinct from sparsity of the original discriminant direction, particularly with dense covariance matrices and strong factors.

The whitening-and-screening procedure is understandable, and the entrywise perturbation analysis targets quantities relevant to support recovery. Retaining information outside the leading principal components is a useful methodological distinction.
The experimental design includes relevant competing classifiers, three synthetic covariance structures, 200 Monte Carlo replications with standard deviations, and two gene-expression applications.
weaknesses: Required: The main consistency claim exceeds the supplied proof. Theorem 3 states almost-sure Bayes consistency under log p=o(n), whereas Section 8.4 concludes convergence in probability of the discriminant score under the stronger condition (log n)(log p)=o(n). The argument does not complete the claimed almost-sure convergence of conditional risk. Strengthen the proof or narrow the theorem and headline claims. Also state explicitly that Assumption 2 keeps sparsity bounded; a growing-sparsity guarantee is not established.

Required: The QDA reduction in Eq. (5.9) is false in general, invalidating the Bayes-consistency conclusion of Theorem 6. Sparse whitened means do not imply that omitted covariance contributions cancel. For example, let u=(0,1,...,1)/sqrt(p-1), Sigma_1=p uu^T+I, Sigma_2=p uu^T+4I, mu_1=e_1, and mu_2=2e_1. Both whitened mean supports equal {1}, satisfying the intended sparsity, spike, and coherence conditions. Nevertheless, the omitted coordinates distinguish the noise variances with error tending to zero, while the selected one-dimensional score has positive optimal error. This extension requires additional structural assumptions, a different procedure, or withdrawal.

Required: Section 5.1 incorrectly identifies Fisher's rule with the Bayes rule for general elliptical distributions and arbitrary class priors. With unequal priors, the likelihood comparison involves log h(q_1)-log h(q_2), which generally does not produce the Gaussian linear boundary. Sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this; bounded Gaussian scale mixtures provide counterexamples. Restrict the distribution/prior assumptions appropriately or establish a valid likelihood-based extension.

Required: The simulation results contain discrepancies that undermine confidence in the comparative evidence. For Model 2, the stated covariance and means give squared Mahalanobis separation 10(1+9 rho)/[(1-rho)(1+19 rho)]. At rho=0.9, the Bayes error is approximately 0.0196%, whereas Table 3 reports an oracle error of 5.40%. This discrepancy cannot reasonably be explained by Monte Carlo variability. Several Table 1 entries also repeat exactly between rho=0.7 and 0.8 despite the changed model. Reconcile the model specification, implementation, and tables, then reassess the accompanying conclusions.

Required: Clarify the whitening estimator. Section 2.3 defines Lambda-hat as the leading eigenvalues of the sample covariance, but Eq. (3.3) adds sigma-hat squared again. Population Lambda contains excess spike eigenvalues, so these definitions are inconsistent. Either subtract the estimated bulk variance when defining the estimated spikes or remove the additional variance term, and make the derivations consistent with the implemented estimator.

Required clarification: Although Section 2 distinguishes original and whitened coordinates, the empirical 'model size' comparisons need the same qualification. A small number of whitened coordinates generally still uses all original measurements through a dense estimated transformation. These counts establish sparsity in different representations and should not be presented as directly comparable original-feature sparsity.

Optional: After resolving the correctness issues, a simulation satisfying all main theoretical assumptions, with varying sample size and dimension, would help connect the theory to practice. Sensitivity to the 90% explained-variance rule for choosing the spike count would also be informative.
